chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, from 'Ubayd ibn Zur'arah, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We are a large household, and sometimes joy and sorrow gather men and women together. Sometimes a woman feels shy to uncover her head in front of the man with whom she shares breastfeeding kinship, and sometimes a man feels it is trivial to look at that. So, what is it that makes breastfeeding prohibitive?' He said: 'That which nourishes flesh and blood.' I said: 'And what is that which nourishes flesh and blood?' He said: 'It was said [that it is] ten sucklings.' I said: 'Does it make prohibitive with ten sucklings?' He said: 'Leave it [alone].' And he said: 'What makes kinship prohibitive, that is what makes breastfeeding prohibitive.' This does not contradict the first report either, because he did not say that ten sucklings make prohibitive by themselves, but rather he attributed it to others, saying: 'It was said.' So if that were authentic, he would have informed about it himself. And that which indicates this is that when the questioner asked him about the authenticity of that, he said to him: 'Leave it.' So if it were authentic, he would have said to him: 'Yes,' and he did not shift his answer to something else for the sake of some expediency.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the number of sucklings required for breastfeeding to establish kinship prohibitions according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the definitive principle that breastfeeding establishes kinship (*mahram*) and the specific numerical threshold of 'ten sucklings,' which he treats as a widely reported tradition (*qala yuqal*) rather than an immutable, self-standing proof. His response 'Leave it' (*da' dha*) upon being asked about its authenticity suggests that while the general rule is certain, the precise number is a matter of scholarly interpretation or practical caution rather than a strict, independent condition. This reflects the Shia scholarly approach of prioritizing the core legal effect over rigid numerical specifications when the textual evidence is not explicit.
